1.d4 f5 2.c4.strategy: The traditional challenge: White takes space, adds control of d5 and aims at a Queen's Gambit-style set-up, with e4 as a later central break. The early c-pawn has a cost: once Black plays ...e6, the f8-bishop can develop with check on b4. The fight is over e4, which Black's f-pawn already watches.

1.d4 f5 2.g3.strategy: Prepares Bg2, which fights for e4 along the long diagonal, and commits White to very little. Castling before c4 keeps Black's bishop from coming to b4 with check. The game becomes a patient fight over e4 and the long diagonal, quieter than after 2.c4.

1.d4 f5 2.Nf3.strategy: A flexible developing move that covers e5 and supports d4. White keeps both a fianchetto and a Queen's Gambit-style c4 available, and can adapt the plan once Black shows which set-up it wants.

1.d4 f5 2.Nc3.name: Dutch Defence: Raphael Variation
1.d4 f5 2.Nc3.strategy: Develops with pressure on e4 and d5 and prepares Bg5 for active piece play; the knight also supports a later e4. The cost is that it blocks the c-pawn, so a Queen's Gambit-style c4 is ruled out for now. A livelier try than the quiet developing moves.

1.d4 f5 2.b3.strategy: Prepares Bb2, which backs up d4 and eyes the long diagonal. It is sound but slower than natural developing moves, and does nothing yet about e4, which Black's f-pawn already controls.

1.d4 f5 2.e3.strategy: Opens the way for the f1-bishop to d3, where it eyes f5. It is sound but passive, since the pawn shuts in the c1-bishop and White does little about e4.

1.d4 f5 2.e4.strategy: Sacrifices a pawn for quick development and play against Black's kingside, weakened along the e8-h5 diagonal. With accurate play the gambit gives White equality at best, so it is a practical weapon rather than a sound main choice.

1.d4 f5 2.h3.name: Dutch Defence: Korchnoi Attack
1.d4 f5 2.h3.background: Carl Mayet introduced the gambit with h3 and g4 against von der Lasa in 1839, and von der Lasa later published analysis of it in the first edition of the Handbuch des Schachspiels. Viktor Korchnoi reintroduced the line into tournament practice in Korchnoi–Känel, Biel 1979.
1.d4 f5 2.h3.strategy: Prepares g4 to break up Black's f5 pawn, a gambit-like try instead of normal development. Black can simply decline and has a good game, so the line works as a surprise weapon rather than a recommended choice.

1.d4 f5 2.Bf4.name: London System
1.d4 f5 2.Bf4.background: The London System takes its name from the London tournament of 1922, where it appeared in seven games, among them games by Capablanca, Alekhine and Rubinstein. James Mason was the first master-level player to use it regularly, including at Vienna 1882, London 1883 and New York 1889.
1.d4 f5 2.Bf4.strategy: Develops the bishop outside the pawn chain and covers e5, a solid set-up that suits many plans. It is quiet and not the most testing: Black can build a Stonewall or a Classical set-up without difficulty.

1.d4 f5 2.Bg5.name: Dutch Defence: Hopton Attack
1.d4 f5 2.Bg5.strategy: Eyes e7 along the d8-h4 diagonal and, after ...Nf6, threatens Bxf6 to double Black's f-pawns, at the cost of the bishop pair. Black equalises with care; a careless kingside advance can run into Qh5 mate along the weakened e8-h5 diagonal.

1.d4 f5 2.Nh3.strategy: Heads for f4 and possibly d3 to help control e5, and keeps f3 free so that a later Bg2 bears on e4. It is sound but rare: the knight starts on the rim and does nothing for the centre yet.

1.d4 f5 2.a3.strategy: Prepares b4 and a queenside space grab, but spends a tempo on a flank move. It does nothing for the centre or for the fight over e4.

1.d4 f5 2.a4.strategy: A slow rook-pawn move that neither develops a piece nor contests e4. It weakens b4 and leaves Black free to develop at will.

1.d4 f5 2.b4.strategy: Grabs queenside space and prepares Bb2, but the pawn is loose: after ...e6 the f8-bishop attacks it, and White must spend another tempo defending it.

1.d4 f5 2.c3.strategy: Supports d4 and opens the d1-a4 diagonal for the queen, but takes c3 from the queen's knight and does nothing to contest e4. A modest move that costs a tempo.

1.d4 f5 2.f3.strategy: Prepares e4, but weakens e3 and the g1-a7 diagonal and takes f3 from the king's knight. White loosens the kingside for little.

1.d4 f5 2.f4.strategy: Mirrors Black's pawn and controls e5, but leaves e3 and e4 without pawn cover for good and weakens the e1-h4 diagonal. Black gets a natural square for a knight on e4 and a comfortable game.

1.d4 f5 2.g4.name: Dutch Defence: Krejcik Gambit
1.d4 f5 2.g4.background: Named after Josef Krejcik (1885–1957), an Austrian chess master, problemist and journalist, who is also remembered for the game known as “The Immortal of Dr. Krejcik”, played against Johann Berger at Carlsbad in 1911.
1.d4 f5 2.g4.strategy: Offers the g-pawn to lure the f5-pawn away from its control of e4. After 2...fxg4 Black keeps e4 under control with a central pawn, which also lets the c8-bishop guard g4.

1.d4 f5 2.h4.strategy: Spends a tempo on a flank pawn that does nothing for the centre or development. It weakens g4 and the kingside, and Black simply develops.

1.d4 f5 2.Nd2.strategy: Prepares e4 with knight support, but blocks the c1-bishop and the queen, and the knight covers less of the centre than from c3. Clumsier than 2.Nf3.

1.d4 f5 2.Na3.strategy: A rim knight heading for c4 or b5, out of play for now and unable to support e4 or the centre.

1.d4 f5 2.Bd2.strategy: Develops passively, blocks the queen's knight from d2 and does not fight for e4.

1.d4 f5 2.Be3.strategy: Develops the bishop but blocks the e-pawn, which makes the usual e3 and Nf3 set-up awkward. White has gained nothing over a quiet Nf3.

1.d4 f5 2.Qd2.strategy: Shuts in the c1-bishop and spends a tempo on an early queen move, with no purpose that a normal developing move would not serve better.

1.d4 f5 2.Qd3.name: Dutch Defence: Alapin Variation
1.d4 f5 2.Qd3.background: Named after Semyon Alapin (1856–1923), a Russian player and openings analyst who also gave his name to variations of the Sicilian, French and Caro-Kann defences. It is also known as the Manhattan Variation.
1.d4 f5 2.Qd3.strategy: Attacks f5 along the b1-h7 diagonal, but Black easily covers the pawn. The early queen move then costs time and blocks the f1-bishop.

1.d4 f5 2.d5.strategy: Gains space at once, but the advanced pawn becomes a target that Black can attack with natural development. The advance also gives up the d-pawn's control of e5 and c5.

1.d4 f5 2.Bh6.strategy: Hangs the bishop to 2...gxh6, and White gets nothing in return.

1.d4 f5 2.Kd2.strategy: Forfeits castling and blocks the queen and the c1-bishop. The king stays in the centre for no gain, and Black develops freely.

1.d4 f5.name: Dutch Defence
1.d4 f5.background: Elias Stein, an Alsatian who settled in The Hague, recommended it as the best reply to 1.d4 in his 1789 book Nouvel essai sur le Jeu des échecs. In the 1951 World Championship match both Mikhail Botvinnik and his challenger David Bronstein played it.

1.d4 f5 2.Bf4 e6.strategy: Supports the f5 pawn and frees the king's bishop, a sound reply to the London bishop. Black gets a compact structure but shuts in its own light-squared bishop, and the bishop on f4 keeps e5 under White's control for now.

1.d4 f5 2.Bf4 Nf6.strategy: Develops the knight to the square that guards e4 and h5, backing up the f-pawn's control of e4. Black meets the London bishop with plain development and keeps every pawn structure open, waiting to see how White commits the centre.

1.d4 f5 2.Bf4 d5.strategy: Grips e4 with a pawn and heads for a wall of pawns, but it walls in the light-squared bishop, and White's bishop on f4 already fights for the e5 square that this structure leaves weak. A solid but passive way to meet the London bishop.

1.d4 f5 2.f4 d5.name: Bird's Opening: Double Duck Formation
1.d4 f5 2.f4 d5.strategy: Takes the centre and the e4 square, mirroring White's pawns: each side's pawns now control the square the other's e-pawn wants to reach. A quiet, manoeuvring game follows, in which neither side can open the centre without preparation.

1.d4 f5 2.f4 Nf6.strategy: Develops the knight and doubles the control of e4, the square the f-pawn fights for. Black keeps the choice of pawn set-up open, while the mirrored pawns leave neither side an obvious edge. A natural, flexible reply.

1.d4 f5 2.f4 e6.strategy: Opens the diagonal of the king's bishop and prepares a solid pawn centre. It leaves e4 to the f-pawn alone, and a later pawn on d5 would shut in the light-squared bishop, so Black chooses solidity over activity.

1.d4 f5 2.g4 fxg4.strategy: Accepts the pawn. Taking gives up the f5 pawn's grip on e4, but White has no easy way to exploit that, and the extra pawn is worth keeping if Black meets the attempts to win it back with care.

1.d4 f5 2.g4 e5.name: Dutch Defence: Hevendehl Gambit
1.d4 f5 2.g4 e5.strategy: A counter-gambit that ignores the offered pawn and hits d4 instead. Both f5 and e5 are attacked and neither is defended, so Black plays for open lines and quick development at the price of material. Sound enough, but riskier than taking or declining the pawn.

1.d4 f5 2.g4 d5.strategy: Declines the pawn and opens the c8 bishop, which now guards f5. If White takes on f5, the bishop recaptures at once; if not, Black keeps the f5 pawn's grip on e4 and a sound centre while White's kingside is loosened by g4.

1.d4 f5 2.g4 fxg4 3.e4.strategy: Opens the queen's attack on g4 and claims the centre, but Black guards g4 with the bishop and hits e4. White keeps open lines and quick development for the pawn, with no sure way to win it back; less direct than the h-pawn attack.

1.d4 f5 2.g4 fxg4 3.h3.strategy: Hits the advanced pawn at once and, once it is taken or exchanged, opens the h-file for the rook. White accepts being a pawn down for quick development and open lines against Black's kingside, the most direct way to play for the compensation the gambit promises.

1.d4 f5 2.g4 fxg4 3.Nc3.strategy: Develops a piece and prepares to take the centre with e4 under the knight's cover. It does not touch the g4-pawn, though, so Black keeps the extra pawn without effort and can complete development in peace; a quiet try for the long term with little compensation yet.

1.d4 f5 2.g4 fxg4 3.e4 d5.strategy: The answer that makes the gambit fail: the pawn opens the c8-bishop's diagonal so g4 stays protected, and it attacks e4 at once. If White takes on d5, the queen recaptures and eyes the h1-rook. Black keeps the extra pawn and the better game.

1.d4 f5 2.g4 fxg4 3.e4 Nf6.strategy: Guards g4 and attacks e4 in one move, but the knight is a poor guard: e5 drives it back to g8 and the queen takes on g4, so the extra pawn goes back and White leads in the centre. Natural, yet it gives the gambit new life.

1.d4 f5 2.g4 fxg4 3.e4 d6.strategy: Opens the c8-bishop's diagonal so that it guards g4, and keeps the pawn without a fight for e4. Solid, but it leaves the e4-pawn alone, so White can finish development at ease and prepare the h-pawn's strike at the g4-pawn.

1.d4 f5 2.g4 fxg4 3.e4 d5 4.Nc3.name: Dutch Defence: Krejcik Gambit, Tate Gambit
1.d4 f5 2.g4 fxg4 3.e4 d5 4.Nc3.strategy: Adds a second attacker to d5 and defends the e4-pawn that Black's d-pawn hits, so White develops with a purpose. Taking on d5 only loses time to the queen's recapture, so keeping the tension is the best way to play for compensation, which White must still find in open play, a pawn down.

1.d4 f5 2.g4 fxg4 3.e4 d5 4.e5.strategy: Pushes the pawn past the d5-pawn instead of defending it, closing the centre and cramping Black's kingside. The pawn is safe, but the c8-bishop still guards g4, so White remains a pawn down with little to attack, and Black simply develops against the chain.

1.d4 f5 2.g4 fxg4 3.e4 d5 4.Bd3.strategy: Develops the bishop and answers ...dxe4 with Bxe4, regaining the central pawn, but ...Nf6 hits the bishop at once and White loses time. Black keeps the extra g-pawn and the c8-bishop still guards g4, so White is a pawn down with less activity than after Nc3.

1.d4 f5 2.h3 Nf6.strategy: The natural reply: the knight develops to its usual Dutch square, guards e4 and adds a second attacker to g4, so White's plan of pushing the g-pawn is no longer free. Black keeps the choice of kingside set-up open.

1.d4 f5 2.h3 d5.strategy: Defends f5 with the c8-bishop and controls e4 with a pawn, so the g-pawn lunge loses its point: if White tries it, Black wins a pawn and the bishop recaptures on g4 with a good game. Black commits to a solid centre and a compact set-up.

1.d4 f5 2.h3 e6.strategy: Defends f5 with a pawn and frees the king's bishop for a compact set-up. The cost is the c8-bishop, shut in behind its own pawns, so a later g4 push is not met by a bishop recapture there and the gambit keeps more bite.

1.d4 f5 2.h3 Nf6 3.g4.name: Dutch Defence: Janzen-Korchnoi Gambit
1.d4 f5 2.h3 Nf6 3.g4.strategy: A gambit that attacks f5 and tries to open the h-file. The pawn is attacked twice and defended once, so Black can answer with ...d5, keeping control of e4, or take it and face dangerous play against h7. Sharp, with a trap waiting for a careless Black.

1.d4 f5 2.h3 Nf6 3.Nf3.strategy: The sound way to continue: the knight develops and the h-pawn already stops ...Ng4. White gives up the surprise of the gambit and its trap, and plays for a normal, flexible game in which nothing is risked.

1.d4 f5 2.h3 Nf6 3.Bg5.strategy: Develops the bishop outside the pawn chain and leans on the f6-knight, and h3 already gives it the retreat to h4. Active, but Black can hit the bishop with ...Ne4 and the bishop may have to move twice, so it is a playable sideline rather than a way to an edge.

1.d4 f5 2.Nc3 Nf6.strategy: Develops the king's knight and puts it on guard over e4 and d5, so White's e-pawn cannot advance without losing a pawn. Black keeps every Dutch set-up open and fights for e4 from the start. The price is a king's side already loosened by the f-pawn, which White's bishop can try to exploit.

1.d4 f5 2.Nc3 e6.strategy: Opens the king's bishop and prepares a solid set-up, but it does nothing for e4. White strikes at once with 3.e4 and, after the exchange, has a knight on a strong central square, the lead in development and the freer game, while Black's light-squared bishop is still shut in.

1.d4 f5 2.Nc3 d5.strategy: Guards e4 with a second pawn but fixes the pawn structure before any piece is out. It leaves e5 as a permanent hole, which 3.Bf4 targets, and weakens e6. White can also offer a gambit pawn in the centre for quick development.

1.d4 f5 2.Nc3 g6.strategy: Heads for a fianchetto but does nothing for e4, and the g-pawn becomes a target: White can strike in the centre at once or go after it with the h-pawn. Black is clearly behind before the bishop arrives.

1.d4 f5 2.Nc3 d6.strategy: Prepares ...e5 and opens the c8-bishop's diagonal, but does nothing for e4. White breaks in the centre at once with 3.e4 and keeps the lead in development and the freer position after the exchange.

1.d4 f5 2.Nc3 c6.strategy: Prepares ...d5 with the c-pawn's support, aiming for a solid pawn wall, but it is too slow and does nothing for e4. White opens the centre at once, and even if Black hits the recaptured knight with ...d5, White stays ahead in development.

1.d4 f5 2.Nc3 b6.strategy: Prepares ...Bb7, which bears on e4 along the long diagonal, but it is slow and develops nothing on the kingside. White opens the centre with 3.e4 before the bishop arrives and stays ahead in development.

1.d4 f5 2.Nc3 c5.strategy: Strikes at d4 before any piece is out, but it is too early. White can close the centre with d5, leaving Black's f-pawn advanced and the pieces undeveloped, or open it with e4, and Black falls behind in development either way.

1.d4 f5 2.Nc3 Nc6.strategy: Hits d4, but 3.d5 drives the knight away. It must retreat again soon after, so Black loses time and cedes central space.

1.d4 f5 2.Nc3 e5.strategy: Gives up a pawn to open the centre: 3.dxe5 takes it, and Black's attempts to regain it cost further time. Black gets some quick development but nothing concrete for the material.

1.d4 f5 2.Nc3 Na6.strategy: Puts the knight on the rim, where its only forward squares are b4 and c5, and does nothing for e4 or d5. White can push e4 at once, without the pawn sacrifice a developed knight would demand.

1.d4 f5 2.Nc3 Nh6.strategy: Heads for f7, where the knight would cover e5 and d6, but on h6 it is exchanged at once: 3.Bxh6 gxh6 wrecks Black's kingside with doubled, isolated h-pawns, and White's e4 then opens the centre against a king that Qh5+ can drive out.

1.d4 f5 2.Nc3 a6.strategy: Takes b5 from the c3-knight and prepares ...b5, but spends a tempo on the flank while Black's development and the centre are still undone, and White is free to take the centre.

1.d4 f5 2.Nc3 a5.strategy: Gains a little queenside space and secures b4 for a knight from a6, but spends a tempo on the flank while the kingside pieces stay at home. White can open the centre with 3.e4 at once.

1.d4 f5 2.Nc3 h6.strategy: Takes g5 from White's bishop, but spends a tempo with nothing developed, and the h6-pawn no longer guards g6. White strikes with e4, and Black cannot hold both the f5-pawn and g6: sooner or later a pawn falls.

1.d4 f5 2.Nc3 h5.strategy: Gains kingside space but develops nothing and leaves g6 without pawn cover. White strikes at once with 3.e4, and Black, with a loosened kingside and no piece out, is soon in serious trouble.

1.d4 f5 2.Nc3 Kf7.strategy: Gives up castling and puts the king where e4 exposes it: after 3.e4 fxe4 4.Nxe4 White has several checks at hand while no black piece is developed.

1.d4 f5 2.Nc3 b5.strategy: Loses a pawn at once: 3.Nxb5 wins it, since nothing protects it, and the knight there also eyes c7. Black has no developed pieces to offer compensation.

1.d4 f5 2.Nc3 g5.strategy: Loses a pawn at once: 3.Bxg5 wins it, since nothing guards g5, and the kingside is weakened for good.

1.d4 f5 2.Nc3 f4.strategy: Gains space but leaves the pawn undefended: 3.Bxf4 wins it along the open c1-h6 diagonal, and Black has no developed piece to offer compensation.

1.d4 f5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.g4.name: Dutch Defence: Spielmann Gambit
1.d4 f5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.g4.strategy: A gambit: g4 hangs to the f-pawn and the knight, but if Black takes it, White builds a broad centre with e4 and plays for the initiative, and the game stays roughly level. It is sound, though White's own kingside is loosened and Black can also decline.

1.d4 f5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.Bg5.strategy: The principled move: the bishop develops outside the pawn chain and attacks the knight that holds e4, putting a question to Black at once. White aims for an active, healthy set-up, and the pressure on f6 can become doubled pawns for Black if the knight is treated carelessly.

1.d4 f5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.Nf3.strategy: Develops the kingside knight, defends d4 and eyes e5, a square the f-pawn can no longer cover once it stands on f5. A flexible, sound set-up that keeps the bishop's post open and asks Black fewer questions than an early bishop sortie.

1.d4 f5 2.Nf3 Nf6.strategy: The natural developing move: the knight takes control of e4, covers h5 and leaves every Dutch set-up open, from a solid pawn chain to a fianchetto of the king's bishop. Black commits to nothing yet, and White has to decide how to meet whichever plan Black picks. The cost is a slower grip on the centre than ...d5 would give at once.

1.d4 f5 2.Nf3 e6.strategy: Opens the f8-bishop and supports a later ...d5, preparing a solid set-up around the e6 and f5 pawns. It often reaches the same positions as developing the knight first. The cost is that the e6-pawn shuts in the c8-bishop, a lasting problem if Black builds a pawn chain on light squares.

1.d4 f5 2.Nf3 d5.strategy: Builds a wall of pawns on d5 and f5 at once, so that e4 is firmly under Black's control. Sound, but it commits the d-pawn before any piece is developed. Since neither the d- nor the f-pawn can ever cover e5, that square becomes a lasting outpost for White's knight.

1.d4 f5 2.Nf3 d6.strategy: Covers e5, so White's knight cannot settle there, opens the c8-bishop's diagonal and prepares a flexible kingside development. Sound but less flexible: the d-pawn commits before the pieces are out, and a pawn wall with ...d5 would now cost a tempo.

1.d4 f5 2.Nf3 g6.strategy: Heads for a kingside fianchetto, putting the bishop on the long diagonal and closing the e8-h5 diagonal. Playable, but less flexible than developing the knight first, since Black commits to the fianchetto before the knight comes out.

1.d4 f5 2.Nf3 c6.strategy: Prepares ...d5 for a solid chain of pawns on c6, d5 and f5, and opens the queen's diagonal toward b6 and a5. Sound but slow: it develops nothing, and the knight and the e-pawn still have to come.

1.d4 f5 2.Nf3 b6.strategy: Prepares ...Bb7, putting the c8-bishop on the long diagonal, where it adds pressure on e4 and eyes the f3-knight. Sound but rare and slow: the kingside is still undeveloped, and White can oppose the bishop with a fianchetto of its own.

1.d4 f5 2.Nf3 c5.strategy: Strikes at d4 before any piece is out. 3.d5 gains space and takes c6 and e6 from Black's pieces, while after 3.dxc5 Black must spend further moves regaining the pawn.

1.d4 f5 2.Nf3 e5.name: Dutch Defence: Omega-Isis Gambit
1.d4 f5 2.Nf3 e5.strategy: Offers the e-pawn at once. After 3.dxe5 Black has quick development and open lines, but they do not make up for the pawn and the loosened kingside.

1.d4 f5 2.Nf3 Nc6.strategy: Develops the knight, but 3.d5 attacks it at once. It cannot step to e5 or d4 without being lost, so it must retreat, and Black has lost time while White's pawn gains space on d5.

1.d4 f5 2.Nf3 Na6.strategy: A rim knight that eyes b4 and c5 but does nothing for the centre or the kingside, and delays Black's development of the kingside. White develops freely.

1.d4 f5 2.Nf3 Nh6.strategy: Allows 3.Bxh6 gxh6, which wrecks Black's kingside pawns; the knight is otherwise badly placed on the rim, with few squares to go to.

1.d4 f5 2.Nf3 a6.strategy: Spends a tempo on a flank pawn that neither develops nor contests the centre, so White simply develops freely.

1.d4 f5 2.Nf3 a5.strategy: Spends a tempo on a flank pawn that develops nothing, contests nothing in the centre and leaves b5 weaker. White gets a free hand in the centre.

1.d4 f5 2.Nf3 h6.strategy: Spends a tempo to stop Bg5, which is no threat yet, and weakens g6. Black falls behind in development while White develops freely.

1.d4 f5 2.Nf3 h5.strategy: Pushes a rim pawn that creates no threat and weakens g5 and g6. White develops freely while Black's knights and bishops are still at home.

1.d4 f5 2.Nf3 b5.strategy: Leaves the b5-pawn undefended: 3.Qd3 attacks it and the f5-pawn at once, and Black cannot hold both. The move develops nothing.

1.d4 f5 2.Nf3 Kf7.strategy: Gives up the right to castle for nothing, develops no piece and walks the king into Ne5+ and an e4 break, with the king far from any shelter.

1.d4 f5 2.Nf3 g5.strategy: Drops a pawn to 3.Nxg5 or 3.Bxg5, since nothing defends it, and the kingside is left full of holes.

1.d4 f5 2.Nf3 f4.strategy: Loses the pawn to 3.Bxf4, because nothing defends it, and gains nothing in space or development in return.

1.d4 f5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.c3.name: Dutch Defence: Barcza Variation
1.d4 f5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.c3.strategy: A quiet move that backs the d4-pawn, so White aims for a slow, flexible set-up instead of challenging the Dutch head on. Safe but modest: it does little against Black's grip on e4, and Black builds the set-up of their choice undisturbed.

1.d4 f5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.g3.strategy: Prepares the fianchetto of the king's bishop, which will fight for e4 and the long diagonal from a distance. White builds a solid, flexible set-up and castles early, accepting a slow game in which both sides develop without contact.

1.d4 f5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Bf4.strategy: Develops the bishop outside the pawn chain, where it controls e5 and the diagonal to c7. A simple, sound system with few theoretical demands: White gets the pieces out and waits to see which set-up Black chooses.

1.d4 f5 2.Qd3 e6.strategy: The soundest way to hold f5: the pawn chain keeps e4 under Black's control and frees the f8-bishop. Black heads for a solid set-up with a firm grip on e4, while White's queen on d3 can come to look misplaced.

1.d4 f5 2.Qd3 g6.strategy: Defends f5 from the side and prepares a bishop on g7, but it weakens the kingside: White's h-pawn can go after the g6-pawn that holds f5. A playable set-up, though Black ends up slightly worse than with the pawn chain.

1.d4 f5 2.Qd3 d5.strategy: Guards f5 with the bishop's diagonal and claims e4 with a second pawn, a firm centre built on solid foundations. The cost is the e5 square: no Black pawn guards it any more, so a White knight can settle there if Black is careless.

1.d4 f5 2.Qd3 d6.strategy: Guards f5 indirectly by opening the c8-bishop's diagonal, and keeps an ...e5 break in reserve. It is a modest way to defend: the bishop is tied to the pawn, and Black does not yet fight for e4 with a second pawn.

1.d4 f5 2.Qd3 d5 3.g4.name: Dutch Defence: Manhattan Gambit, Anti-Stonewall
1.d4 f5 2.Qd3 d5 3.g4.strategy: Attacks f5 a second time, with pawn and queen against the single defence of the bishop, so Black must settle the tension at once. A tricky gambit: White opens lines at the cost of a loosened kingside, and a pawn.

1.d4 f5 2.Qd3 d5 3.Nf3.strategy: Develops the knight and calms the position, where the g4 lunge forces matters at the cost of a pawn. White needs pieces out more than a quick attack, since the queen already stands on the f1-bishop's best square.

1.d4 f5 2.Qd3 d5 3.Nc3.strategy: Develops the queen's knight and puts pressure on d5, so Black has to support the d-pawn. It blocks White's own c-pawn, which rules out the usual queenside expansion, but it is a natural, flexible developing move.

1.d4 f5 2.Qd3 d6 3.g4.name: Dutch Defence: Manhattan Gambit, Anti-Modern
1.d4 f5 2.Qd3 d6 3.g4.strategy: Attacks f5 twice while only the c8-bishop defends it, so Black has to react immediately. It is a gambit lunge: if Black takes, the queen eyes the open diagonal to h7, but White's kingside is loosened and a pawn has been given.

1.d4 f5 2.Qd3 d6 3.Nf3.strategy: Develops the knight and takes e5 under control, which makes Black's natural central advance harder. White puts development before the gambit, a sound way to make something of an eccentric early queen move.

1.d4 f5 2.Qd3 d6 3.Bf4.strategy: Puts the bishop on its best diagonal before the pawns close it in, with pressure on d6, the pawn that holds Black's centre together. Active and low-risk, and it keeps the gambit in reserve.

1.d4 f5 2.Qd3 d6 3.Nc3.strategy: Develops the queen's knight and, with the queen already on d3, prepares the central strike e4. White builds its centre by sound development instead of a pawn sacrifice, and the early queen move starts to look purposeful.

1.d4 f5 2.Qd3 e6 3.g4.name: Dutch Defence: Manhattan Gambit, Anti-Classical Line
1.d4 f5 2.Qd3 e6 3.g4.strategy: Hits f5 a second time, which the e6-pawn alone cannot hold. If Black takes the pawn, the queen eyes h7 along the open diagonal, but the g-pawn is gone and, without a follow-up, White is simply a pawn down.

1.d4 f5 2.Qd3 e6 3.Nf3.strategy: Develops the knight and meets Black's compact set-up with ordinary play. The early queen move did little except take the f1-bishop's diagonal, so White needs the pieces out first, with the g4 lunge kept in reserve.

1.d4 f5 2.Qd3 e6 3.Bf4.strategy: Develops the bishop to an active diagonal outside the pawn chain, where it controls e5, the square in front of Black's e-pawn. A sound, low-risk system: White gets the pieces out and waits for Black to show a plan.

1.d4 f5 2.Qd3 g6 3.g4.name: Dutch Defence: Manhattan Gambit, Anti-Leningrad
1.d4 f5 2.Qd3 g6 3.g4.strategy: Attacks f5 twice against the single defence of the g6-pawn, so Black must settle the tension. The lunge gambits a pawn for open lines against a fianchetto set-up that has not yet castled, and it loosens White's own kingside in the process.

1.d4 f5 2.Qd3 g6 3.Nf3.strategy: Develops the knight and covers e5 and g5. It is sound, but it ignores what ...g6 has loosened: the pawn that holds f5 can be attacked by the h-pawn, and quiet development lets Black settle the kingside at no cost.

1.d4 f5 2.Qd3 g6 3.Nc3.strategy: Develops the queen's knight against e4, the square the f5-pawn is meant to control, so queen and knight both stand behind a possible central strike. Sound and natural, though the knight blocks White's own c-pawn.

1.d4 f5 2.Qd3 g6 3.h4.strategy: Goes after the g6-pawn that holds f5: h5 is coming, so Black has to meet the threat at once. White keeps the initiative and a lasting edge, since the weakened kingside leaves Black no easy way to hit back.
